nodes.question: How do the analyses of Zhou et al. (2023) and Duqi (2023) differ in terms of their depth and structure?
nodes.answer: The analyses of Zhou et al. (2023) and Duqi (2023) are broad, shallow, and unstructured, lacking the systematic coverage of intricacies and heterogeneities within the banking sector.
nodes.paragraph: While these studies provide insights into the real economic impacts of disasters and climate transition risks, existing literature has not made sufficient efforts to understand the complex interactions between physical climate and natural hazard shocks, banks, and the real economy. In the works closest to mine, Zhou et al. (2023) and Duqi (2023) provide excellent but very broad overviews. In particular, Zhou et al. (2023) cover insurance, equity markets, bond markets, international financial flows, and the banking sector, making it suitable as a first introduction to various general aspects of the literature. The textbook of Duqi (2023) provides regulatory context and discusses foundational theories, making it useful for instance for educational purposes. However, due to the scope of these studies, the analyses remain shallow and unstructured and do not systematically cover the intricacies and heterogeneities within the banking sector that are necessary to understand to guide future research and give context-sensitive policy recommendations Therefore, this review contributes an in-depth, systematic analysis of the empirical evidence on the bank-level impacts of natural hazard shocks, and the channels through which banks mediate the real economic consequences.

nodes.question: What are the three functions of money as defined by Aristotle?
nodes.answer: The three functions of money as defined by Aristotle are as a medium of exchange, a store of value, and a unit of account.
nodes.paragraph: Beyond its three func- tions as defined by Aristotle namely the role of medium of exchange, store of value and unit of account money might play a role in communication and in the creation of social bonds or signs of belonging to a society. nodes.question: How has the emergence of alternative currencies been characterized since the end of the twentieth century?
nodes.answer: The emergence of alternative currencies has been characterized as an unprecedented phenomenon in the monetary history of industrial societies.
nodes.paragraph: Yet, most orthodox economists affix a neutrality to it, both from economic and social points of view. In that vein, money is approached from a functional and technical angle (Fare 2016) devoid of any political aspect. Fare and Ahmed (2018) note that conventional economics pays marginal attention to alternative currencies, i.e. curren- cies that are alternatives or complements to mainstream state fiat currencies and that have limited functions and circuits of circulation. Indeed, conventional economics struggles to measure the impacts of alternative currencies because it is based on theoretical and normative conceptions of money that do not allow it to understand their heterogeneity, their characteristics and their usefulness at the local level. Since the creation in 1934 of the WIR (an independent comple- mentary currency system in Switzerland) and the establish - ment of a local exchange trading system (in Vancouver, Canada, in 1983), the emergence of alternative currencies has accelerated from the end of the twentieth century (Blanc 2018). The continuous development of alternative curren- cies can be seen as an unprecedented phenomenon on the scale of the monetary history of industrial societies (Blanc 2018).

nodes.question: What type of model is employed in the macroeconomic component of the framework?
nodes.answer: A dynamic general equilibrium model (CGE) is employed in the macroeconomic component.
nodes.paragraph: This approach provides a robust analytical tool for designing more effective public policies that strengthen resilience and mitigate the effects of climate disasters on food security. 1 3 Economic and Food Security Impacts of Climate Disasters and Mitigation The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Sect. 2 describes the data and the methodological framework. Section 3 discusses the simulations and results. Section 4 out- lines the policy implications of the findings and Sect. 5 concludes the paper. 2 Data and Methodological Framework The methodological framework uses a top-down macro-micro modeling approach to deter - mine the changes in the economy and food security due to climate disasters in Nigeria. We use a dynamic general equilibrium model (CGE) in the macroeconomic component. Then, the macro-simulation results are broken down at the household level by rural or urban areas and regions in a microsimulation module. The micro model is used to assess the impact of climate shocks on consumption, food security, and food poverty. 2.1 Data Sources The data for the CGE model is the 2019 Social Accounting Matrix (SAM) constructed by Mitik et al.
